cases.n: IICSA — sexual abuse of children in custodial institutions, 2009–2017
cases.victims_note: More than 1,000 incidents of alleged sexual abuse in custody were reported between 2009 and 2017; this is a count of incidents, not of children.
cases.who: Young offender institutions and secure training centres in England and Wales (incl. Medway and Rainsbrook STCs)
cases.d: The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse published its report on children in custodial institutions on 28 February 2019, after public hearings on 9–20 July 2018. It found that more than 1,000 incidents of alleged sexual abuse were reported in custody from 2009 to 2017, far more than official figures showed, and that children in young offender institutions and secure training centres remained at risk. Recent cases included staff touching detainees during searches and restraint; adult survivors also described abuse in custody decades earlier.
cases.cite: IICSA, Sexual Abuse of Children in Custodial Institutions: 2009–2017, Investigation Report, 28 February 2019

cases.n: IICSA — the internet and child sexual abuse (2020)
cases.who: Online platforms and services (Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat named); UK government and law enforcement
cases.d: IICSA's report on the internet, published 12 March 2020, found that millions of indecent images of children are in circulation and that most are on mainstream platforms such as Facebook, Instagram and Snapchat, not only the dark web. It cited BT data of more than 30,000 attempts every 24 hours to view abuse material, and an NSPCC estimate that about 500,000 men in the UK had viewed such images. It recommended pre-screening of uploads, stricter age verification and international action to remove images hosted abroad.
cases.cite: IICSA, The Internet, Investigation Report, 12 March 2020 (summary by Switalskis solicitors)

cases.n: IICSA — sexual abuse in residential, boarding, music and special schools (2022)
cases.who: Boarding schools, residential special schools and specialist music schools in England and Wales; school inspectorates and the Teaching Regulation Agency
cases.d: IICSA's residential schools report (March 2022, over 220 pages) covered music and residential special schools in phase 1 and day and boarding schools in phase 2. It found that boarding pupils, children with special needs and pupils in one-to-one music teaching were especially exposed to abuse by adults and peers, and that school reputations were sometimes put before victims. It found weaknesses in inspection, teacher regulation and DBS checks and made recommendations in seven areas.
cases.cite: IICSA, Sexual abuse and exploitation of children in residential schools, Investigation Report, March 2022 (summary by Farrer & Co)

cases.n: IICSA — child sexual exploitation by organised networks (six areas, 2022)
cases.place: England and Wales (St Helens, Tower Hamlets, Swansea, Durham, Bristol, Warwickshire)
cases.who: Organised networks exploiting children; local authorities and police forces in six case-study areas
cases.cover: Victims were sometimes treated as offenders while perpetrators were often not investigated or prosecuted.
cases.d: IICSA's report of 1 February 2022 examined St Helens, Tower Hamlets, Swansea, Durham, Bristol and Warwickshire and found that network exploitation occurs in all parts of England and Wales and that councils and police showed extensive failures. Officials had wrongly assumed exploitation was declining; it had become more hidden, including through phones, apps and live-streaming for payment. None of the six areas recorded the ethnicity of victims or alleged perpetrators. It made six recommendations, including mandatory data collection.
cases.cite: IICSA, Child sexual exploitation by organised networks, Investigation Report, 1 February 2022 (HC 1059)

cases.n: IICSA — Ealing Abbey and St Benedict's School (Benedictine)
cases.victims_note: Since 2003 four staff connected to St Benedict's were convicted of offences involving more than 20 children; at least 18 further allegations were received.
cases.who: Ealing Abbey (English Benedictine Congregation) and St Benedict's School
cases.cover: IICSA found a culture of cover-up and denial; very senior figures were perpetrators and staff were warned to stay silent; the abbot's responses were seriously deficient.
cases.d: IICSA's report of 24 October 2019 found abuse at St Benedict's School over more than 30 years, in a 'sadistic and predatory' atmosphere where corporal punishment was often used to facilitate sexual abuse. Since 2003 four people connected to the school had been convicted of offences against more than 20 children, and the inquiry received at least 18 further allegations against them and eight other monks and teachers. It found Abbot Martin Shipperlee's responses seriously deficient; he resigned during the investigation.
cases.cite: IICSA, Roman Catholic Church: English Benedictine Congregation case study — Ealing Abbey and St Benedict's School, 24 October 2019

cases.n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — child migrants sent from Scotland (Case Study 8)
cases.who: Charities, religious orders and governments that ran child migration schemes from Scotland to Canada and Australia
cases.d: Lady Smith published the first volume of findings on child migration on 21 March 2023 and a second volume in September 2023. She found that many thousands of children were sent from Scotland, mainly to Canada and later Australia, and that some were sexually abused at their destinations, including by men in holy orders and by members of a paedophile ring. About 80,000 children were sent from the UK to Canada by 1920 and about 7,000 to Australia between 1912 and 1970; 45 people gave evidence.
cases.cite: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry, Case Study no. 8, Volume 1 (21 March 2023) and Volume 2 (28 September 2023)

cases.n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Morrison's Academy, Crieff
cases.who: Morrison's Academy boarding houses
cases.d: The Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry's eleventh set of findings, published in March 2024, covered boarding at Morrison's Academy from 1945 to 2007. Lady Smith found children were abused, mainly physically and emotionally, with some sexual abuse, including by a few older pupils. Boarding houses were run as largely unsupervised 'fiefdoms' until the 1990s and a strong culture of not reporting discouraged children from speaking up.
cases.cite: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry, Case Study no. 9 findings: Morrison's Academy, March 2024

cases.n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Queen Victoria School, Dunblane (military boarding school)
cases.who: Queen Victoria School (Ministry of Defence boarding school for children of service personnel)
cases.d: The inquiry's thirteenth volume of findings, published 22 October 2024, found 'dreadful abuse' at Queen Victoria School, especially from the late 1950s to the early 1990s, with weak oversight and a military culture of silence. A teacher employed 1973–1993 groomed and sexually abused several primary-age boys and the school did not act on his well-known behaviour. A drumming instructor sexually abused seven female pupils between 2011 and 2019, after child protection systems were in place.
cases.cite: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry, Case Study no. 9 findings: Queen Victoria School, 22 October 2024

cases.n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Keil School, Dumbarton
cases.who: Keil School (closed 2000); Mackinnon-Macneill Trust
cases.cover: A parent's early complaint about the physics teacher was inadequately investigated and covered up by the headmaster and other senior staff; the school's reputation was put before children.
cases.d: The fifteenth volume of findings, published 20 August 2025, found abusive practices normalised at Keil School from the late 1950s to the 1980s. Physics teacher William Bain (at Keil 1987–2000) sexually abused many children, some almost daily, after a parent's early complaint was covered up by the headmaster and senior staff; Bain was convicted in 2016 and again on 30 June 2025. An English teacher, David Gutteridge, was convicted in 2024 of abusing a pupil. Publication was delayed at the Crown's request until Bain's trial ended.
cases.cite: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry, Case Study no. 9 findings: Keil School, 20 August 2025

cases.n: Scotland — Shaw historical abuse systemic review (residential care 1950–1995)
cases.who: Residential schools and children's homes in Scotland (e.g. Nazareth House Kilmarnock, Quarriers Village); successive governments and local authorities
cases.d: Tom Shaw, former chief inspector of education in Northern Ireland, reviewed for the Scottish Executive the laws, rules and records governing residential schools and children's homes from 1950 to 1995; his report was published in November 2007. Survivors described mental, physical and sexual abuse. Shaw found the regulations were extensive but successive governments and authorities failed to make sure they were followed, and that abuse would likely have been lower had they been applied. About 35 survivors were interviewed and about 80 other people gave evidence.
cases.cite: Historical Abuse Systemic Review (Tom Shaw) for the Scottish Executive, November 2007; The Scotsman; Community Care

cases.n: Kerelaw residential school and secure unit, Stevenston — Frizzell inquiry
cases.victims_note: Glasgow City Council reported 350–400 allegations from 159 people in 2007.
cases.who: Kerelaw residential school and secure unit, run by Glasgow City Council from 1996
cases.d: The Scottish Government commissioned Eddie Frizzell to inquire into Kerelaw in November 2007; his report was published in May 2009. It found abuse did take place, physical abuse was prevalent, complaints were not consistently followed up, and there were significant failures of management and leadership linked to Glasgow City Council's neglect of the school. Two staff were convicted in 2006, one receiving 10 years for 18 offences, and 14 staff were dismissed. The council had reported 350–400 allegations from 159 people.
cases.cite: Independent Inquiry into Abuse at Kerelaw Residential School and Secure Unit (Frizzell), May 2009, via Scottish Law blog 12 May 2009

cases.n: Catholic Church in Scotland — McLellan Commission (2015)
cases.who: Catholic Church in Scotland (Bishops' Conference of Scotland)
cases.cover: The report described a culture of denial and inadequate support for victims.
cases.d: The Bishops' Conference of Scotland set up a commission chaired by Andrew McLellan in November 2013; its report on safeguarding policy and practice was published on 18 August 2015. It stated that there was no doubt that abuse 'of the most serious kind' had taken place in the Scottish Catholic Church, restated the culture of denial and inadequate support for victims, and made recommendations. Its remit did not include naming individuals; the bishops apologised to survivors.
cases.cite: A Review of the Current Safeguarding Policies, Procedures and Practice within the Catholic Church in Scotland (McLellan Report), 18 August 2015

cases.n: Scottish FA — Independent Review of Sexual Abuse in Scottish Football (2021)
cases.who: Scottish football: Scottish FA and clubs including Celtic, Rangers and Hibernian (named among clubs asked to apologise)
cases.d: The independent review chaired by Martin Henry, commissioned by the Scottish FA, published its final report on 11 February 2021 after being held back for criminal proceedings. It examined non-recent abuse mainly from the 1970s to the early 1990s and found that abusers were able to move through Scottish football and keep their activities hidden, with flawed decisions that sometimes meant little or no action. 33 people gave personal accounts; the review asked clubs to apologise, and the Scottish FA apologised.
cases.cite: Independent Review of Sexual Abuse in Scottish Football, final report, 11 February 2021

cases.n: Northern Ireland — Marshall independent inquiry into child sexual exploitation (2014)
cases.victims_note: 100–145 children identified at significant risk; the report said the real number was likely 'significantly higher'.
cases.who: Individuals and groups exploiting children in Northern Ireland, some using purported paramilitary links; children in residential care
cases.d: Health minister Edwin Poots commissioned Professor Kathleen Marshall after the PSNI said in September 2013 it was investigating the suspected exploitation of 22 young people. Her report, published 18 November 2014, identified 100 to 145 children at significant risk of sexual exploitation and said the real number was likely much higher. It found individuals with purported paramilitary links used fear to exploit young people, but no targeting by paramilitary groups as such, and no evidence of cover-up. It made 17 key recommendations.
cases.cite: Child Sexual Exploitation in Northern Ireland: Report of the Independent Inquiry (Marshall), 18 November 2014; Irish Times

cases.n: Clwyd children's homes — Jillings report (1996, published 2013)
cases.victims_note: At least 24 victims identified; 3,755 witness statements were taken by North Wales Police.
cases.who: Clwyd County Council children's homes; North Wales Police
cases.cover: Compiled in 1996 but withheld for 17 years; the panel said agencies gave limited information and sometimes refused to meet it; North Wales Police investigated allegations against its own officers.
cases.d: John Jillings, a former director of social services, led an investigation into Clwyd's residential units; the report was finished in 1996 and published in redacted form in July 2013. It found abuse of children in Clwyd homes was 'extensive' over many years and that responses were 'too little and too late'. It criticised North Wales Police for investigating allegations against its own officers and said the council and other agencies limited the investigation. It called for a judicial inquiry, which became the Waterhouse Inquiry.
cases.cite: Jillings report on Clwyd children's homes (1996), published by the six North Wales councils, July 2013; The Scotsman

cases.n: Macur Review of the Waterhouse Inquiry (North Wales, 2016)
cases.who: Waterhouse Inquiry (Lost in Care); North Wales children's homes
cases.d: The UK government set up the Macur Review in 2012 to check whether the Waterhouse Inquiry into abuse in North Wales children's homes had been given all relevant material and had investigated within its terms. Lady Justice Macur reported in March 2016 and found no evidence of significant failings that would undermine Waterhouse's findings. She made six recommendations, the last advising caution about re-opening past inquiries.
cases.cite: The Report of the Macur Review, March 2016 (UK Government)

cases.n: Clywch inquiry — Children's Commissioner for Wales on Ysgol Gyfun Rhydfelen
cases.who: Ysgol Gyfun Rhydfelen (secondary school); Mid Glamorgan County Council education department
cases.cover: In 1991 an education officer failed to make a child protection referral despite pupils' statements; the director of education obstructed a proper investigation, issued a misleading statement and let the teacher resign without action.
cases.d: The first inquiry by the Children's Commissioner for Wales, Peter Clarke, published in 2004, concluded that drama teacher John Owen committed serious acts of sexual impropriety against pupils at Ysgol Gyfun Rhydfelen. Owen was charged in 2001 after four former pupils went to police and died before trial. The commissioner found that when sixth-formers complained in 1991 no child protection referral was made and the county's director of education obstructed a proper investigation. It recommended independent school disciplinary tribunals for Wales.
cases.cite: Children's Commissioner for Wales, Clywch: Report of the examination of the Children's Commissioner for Wales into allegations of child sexual abuse in a school setting, 2004; Community Care

cases.n: Leicestershire children's homes — Frank Beck and the Kirkwood Inquiry
cases.place: Leicestershire (The Poplars, Ratcliffe Road, The Beeches)
cases.victims_note: Beck's 1991 sentencing covered assaults on more than 100 children; police took statements from nearly 400.
cases.who: Leicestershire County Council Social Services; officer-in-charge Frank Beck
cases.d: Frank Beck ran three Leicestershire council children's homes between 1973 and 1986 and resigned in March 1986 after a complaint by two male staff. On 29 November 1991 he received five life sentences for offences including rape covering more than 100 children; police took statements from nearly 400. The Leicestershire inquiry chaired by Andrew Kirkwood QC, reported in 1993, was strongly critical of how the county's social services were managed in the 1970s and 1980s and of several senior managers. Its hearings were held in private.
cases.cite: The Leicestershire Inquiry 1992 (Andrew Kirkwood QC), published 1993; Leicester Crown Court verdict 29 Nov 1991 (via Wikipedia 'Frank Beck')

cases.n: Utting review 'People Like Us' — safeguards for children living away from home (1997)
cases.place: England and Wales (Department of Health, London)
cases.who: Children's homes, foster care, boarding and special schools, penal institutions in England and Wales
cases.d: After allegations of widespread ill-treatment in children's homes dating back to the 1970s, the government asked Sir William Utting, former chief inspector of social services, to review safeguards for all children living away from home. His 1997 report found safeguards stronger than a decade earlier but said children in prison and in private foster care were not properly protected and that abuse of disabled children was overlooked; it called persistent sexual abusers 'a scourge of childhood'. It made 159 recommendations, leading to the Quality Protects programme.
cases.cite: People Like Us: The Report of the Review of the Safeguards for Children Living Away from Home (Utting), 1997; Community Care

cases.n: UK government study of 'satanic ritual abuse' claims — La Fontaine report (1994)
cases.who: Claims of organised satanic/ritual abuse made in 84 cases, including those that led to removals of children in Rochdale and Orkney
cases.d: Health Secretary Virginia Bottomley commissioned anthropologist Jean La Fontaine in 1991 after children were removed from homes in Rochdale and Orkney on claims of ritual abuse. Her report, made public on 3 June 1994, examined 84 cases and found no evidence supporting any allegation of satanic abuse. Only three claims of 'ritual' abuse were substantiated, and she said even those did not merit that description.
cases.cite: J. S. La Fontaine, The Extent and Nature of Organised and Ritual Abuse, Department of Health, 1994; Cult Education Institute archive of 3 June 1994 report

cases.n: Wanless–Whittam review — Home Office files on organised abuse claims (2014)
cases.who: Home Office; Geoffrey Dickens MP's 1980s dossier; Paedophile Information Exchange funding claims
cases.cover: 114 relevant Home Office files were missing, lost or destroyed; the review could not rule out that some were removed to hide abuse.
cases.d: Peter Wanless and Richard Whittam QC reviewed, for the Home Secretary, how the Home Office handled information about organised child abuse in the 1980s, including Geoffrey Dickens MP's dossier. Their report, submitted 15 October 2014 and published 11 November 2014, found no evidence of an organised Home Office effort to hide child abuse, but said 114 files were missing, lost or destroyed and the imperfect records meant removal to hide abuse could not be ruled out. It found nothing to support claims that the Home Office funded the Paedophile Information Exchange.
cases.cite: An Independent Review of Two Home Office Commissioned Independent Reviews Looking at Information Held in Connection with Child Abuse from 1979–1999 (Wanless and Whittam), November 2014; The Scotsman

cases.n: Savile in schools and children's homes — 14 investigations with independent oversight (2015)
cases.who: 14 councils, charities and schools (incl. Barnardo's, Action for Children, Henshaws Society for Blind People, Sevenoaks School) named in information about Jimmy Savile
cases.d: After Michael Gove's statement of 27 March 2014, 14 organisations investigated information linking Jimmy Savile to their children's homes and schools from the 1960s to the 1980s. Lucy Scott-Moncrieff's independent oversight report, published by the Department for Education on 26 February 2015, found the investigations were conducted appropriately but could not reach firm conclusions: many informants were judged credible, but there was not enough corroborating evidence for definite findings.
cases.cite: Independent oversight of investigations into matters relating to Jimmy Savile at schools and children's homes (Scott-Moncrieff), DfE written statement, 26 February 2015

cases.n: Children's Commissioner for England — inquiry into sexual exploitation in gangs and groups (2012–13)
cases.place: England (Office of the Children's Commissioner, London)
cases.victims_note: 2,409 children confirmed as victims in the 14 months August 2010 – October 2011; a further 16,500 judged at high risk.
cases.who: Gangs and groups sexually exploiting children across England
cases.d: The Office of the Children's Commissioner's inquiry, with the University of Bedfordshire, published interim findings on 21 November 2012. It identified 2,409 children confirmed as victims of sexual exploitation by gangs and groups in the 14 months from August 2010 to October 2011, and a further 16,500 at high risk. It recorded 1,514 perpetrators of varied ethnicity (545 white, 415 Asian, 244 black, the rest unknown) and found warning signs were routinely missed. The final report followed in 2013.
cases.cite: Office of the Children's Commissioner, 'I thought I was the only one': Inquiry into Child Sexual Exploitation in Gangs and Groups, interim report, 21 November 2012; Children & Young People Now

cases.n: CEOP thematic assessment 'Out of mind, out of sight' — localised grooming (2011)
cases.who: Groups grooming children in person ('localised grooming'); Local Safeguarding Children Boards
cases.d: The Child Exploitation and Online Protection Centre announced in January 2011 a thematic assessment of 'localised grooming' and published 'Out of mind, out of sight' later that year. It recorded 2,379 cases since the start of 2008, mostly involving men aged 18 to 24 (ethnicity, where known: 38% white, 26% Asian, 3% black), with about 90% of victims white. It found two-thirds of Local Safeguarding Children Boards were not meeting national guidance and that victims did not expect to be believed. CEOP warned the data were incomplete.
cases.cite: CEOP, Out of Mind, Out of Sight: Breaking down the barriers to understanding child sexual exploitation, 2011; Yorkshire Post

cases.n: House of Commons Home Affairs Committee — child sexual exploitation and localised grooming (2013)
cases.who: Police, social services and the Crown Prosecution Service; Rochdale and Rotherham councils
cases.d: The Home Affairs Committee's report of 10 June 2013 (HC 68-I) found that police, social services and the Crown Prosecution Service had failed vulnerable children in some areas and that this was still happening across the country. It found Rochdale and Rotherham councils slow to recognise organised abuse of children, many in council care, and blamed a lack of professional curiosity. It described a model of localised grooming involving mainly Pakistani-heritage men targeting young white girls but warned against focusing on that model alone, and recommended court reforms.
cases.cite: House of Commons Home Affairs Committee, Child sexual exploitation and the response to localised grooming, Second Report of Session 2013–14, HC 68-I, 10 June 2013

cases.n: Rotherham — Casey inspection of the council (2015)
cases.who: Rotherham Metropolitan Borough Council
cases.cover: Inspectors found the council went to 'some lengths' to cover up information and silence whistleblowers, and used severance payments and compromise agreements instead of holding staff to account.
cases.d: Louise Casey's government-ordered inspection, published 4 February 2015, judged Rotherham council 'not fit for purpose' and in denial about continuing failures after the Jay report. It found the council still treated child sexual exploitation as a social care issue, could not assure the public that taxi licence holders were fit and proper (86% of audited complaint investigations were inadequate), and had covered up information and silenced whistleblowers. The council leader and cabinet resigned and the government sent in commissioners.
cases.cite: Report of Inspection of Rotherham Metropolitan Borough Council (Louise Casey), 4 February 2015; Children & Young People Now

cases.n: Manchester — Operation Augusta assurance review (2020)
cases.victims_note: At least 57 victims (girls aged 12–16) and 97 potential suspects identified by Operation Augusta; the later Operation Green Jacket identified 53 potential victims, 48 of them in council care.
cases.who: Greater Manchester Police; Manchester City Council children's homes; groups of men exploiting girls in care
cases.cover: Senior officers closed and under-resourced the investigation in 2005; minutes of the closure meetings disappeared and several officials declined to cooperate with the review.
cases.d: An assurance review commissioned by Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham, published 14 January 2020, found that Operation Augusta, set up in 2004 after the death of a 15-year-old girl in care, had identified at least 57 victims and 97 potential suspects before senior officers closed it down in 2005. Allegations of rape and abuse were not followed up and very few perpetrators were brought to justice; some suspects visited council children's homes apparently with staff knowledge. Minutes of the closure meetings were missing.
cases.cite: Greater Manchester Combined Authority, An Assurance Review of Operation Augusta (Newsam and Ridgway), January 2020; ITV News, 14 January 2020

cases.n: Ofsted review of sexual abuse in schools and colleges (2021)
cases.who: Schools and colleges in England (state and private)
cases.d: After thousands of anonymous accounts were posted to the Everyone's Invited website, the government asked Ofsted to review sexual abuse in schools and colleges. Its report of 10 June 2021, based on visits to 32 schools and colleges and talks with more than 900 young people, found sexual harassment had become normalised: 79% of girls said sexual assault of any kind happens often between peers and 64% said unwanted touching does. Many teachers underestimated the problem and pupils saw no point in reporting.
cases.cite: Ofsted, Review of sexual abuse in schools and colleges, 10 June 2021; ITV News

cases.n: Church of England — second Past Cases Review (PCR2, 2022)
cases.victims_note: 383 new cases; 168 involved children, 149 vulnerable adults, 27 both, 39 unrecorded.
cases.who: Church of England dioceses, cathedrals and national institutions
cases.cover: Allegations were often handled informally, without investigation, records or referral to safeguarding professionals.
cases.d: The Church of England's second Past Cases Review, reported nationally on 5 October 2022, examined more than 75,000 files, some from the 1940s, and identified 383 new cases: 168 involved children, 149 vulnerable adults and 27 both. 242 cases involved clergy, 53 other church officers and 41 volunteers working with children. It found allegations had often been handled informally without proper investigation or referral, and made 26 national recommendations. The archbishops apologised.
cases.cite: Church of England, Past Cases Review 2: national report, 5 October 2022

cases.n: Isle of Man — Knottfield children's home (Tynwald committee report)
cases.who: Knottfield children's home (Isle of Man Government); house parent Joseph Marshall
cases.d: A Tynwald scrutiny committee (Social Affairs Policy Review Committee) chaired by David Cretney reported in October 2018 on 'horrific physical, emotional and sexual abuse' at Knottfield children's home between 1973 and 1983, when Joseph Marshall ran it, and found the authorities had failed the children. Marshall was convicted of 13 offences in 1992 and jailed again for six years in April 2022 for sexually abusing two boys there. The report was withdrawn during the criminal case; the Isle of Man Government apologised on 16 January 2023 and accepted all 11 recommendations.
cases.cite: Tynwald Social Affairs Policy Review Committee report on Knottfield, October 2018; Isle of Man Government statement, 16 January 2023; Manx Radio

cases.n: Ireland — National Board's safeguarding reviews of every Catholic diocese and order (2011–2017), incl. Raphoe
cases.place: All dioceses on the island of Ireland (National Board, Maynooth); Raphoe review covers Co. Donegal
cases.victims_note: Raphoe: 52 allegations against 14 priests since 1975; four priests convicted. Other dioceses reported separately (e.g. Kerry 67 allegations, Down and Connor 59).
cases.who: Catholic dioceses and religious congregations in Ireland and Northern Ireland; National Board for Safeguarding Children in the Catholic Church
cases.cover: Raphoe: the review found 'significant' errors by bishops, with frequent delays in reporting allegations or none at all, and victims' needs ignored to protect the Church's reputation (Bishop Boyce's statement).
cases.d: The Catholic Church's National Board for Safeguarding Children reviewed every diocese on the island of Ireland and the religious orders that ran schools and institutions, publishing in tranches from 30 November 2011 to 2017. The first tranche included Raphoe, where 52 allegations had been made against 14 priests since 1975 and four had been convicted; Bishop Philip Boyce accepted 'very poor judgements and mistakes'. A December 2013 tranche reported, for example, 67 allegations against 21 priests in Kerry and 59 against 42 in Down and Connor.
cases.cite: NBSCCCI Review of Safeguarding Practice in the Diocese of Raphoe, 30 November 2011; NBSCCCI reviews of six dioceses, December 2013 (Irish Times)

cases.n: Ireland — Murphy inquiry into child sexual abuse in swimming (1998)
cases.victims_note: Coach Derry O'Rourke pleaded guilty to 29 specimen charges involving 11 girls; gardaí said up to 30 children may have been abused.
cases.who: Irish Amateur Swimming Association (IASA); national coaches including Derry O'Rourke and George Gibney (Gibney never tried)
cases.cover: The report found 'total systems failure' in the IASA; charges against another coach were dropped after a 1994 judicial review because of delay.
cases.d: The Irish government asked senior counsel Roderick Murphy to inquire after former Olympic coach Derry O'Rourke was jailed for 12 years for abusing 11 girl swimmers. His 165-page report (1998) found that children had come to believe abuse was a normal part of training, and described ineptitude and total systems failure in the Irish Amateur Swimming Association. It reported two previously unidentified coaches under Garda investigation and made more than 100 recommendations; the government cut the association's funding.
cases.cite: Report of the Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse in Swimming (Murphy), 1998; Irish Echo; Irish Times

cases.n: Madonna House residential centre, Dublin — Department of Health inquiry (1996)
cases.who: Madonna House children's residential centre, run by the Sisters of Charity
cases.cover: Management failed to act on staff concerns and children's complaints; one staff member regarded as having an inappropriate relationship with a girl was paid to live elsewhere but kept his job; the sections describing abuse were removed from the published 1996 report and only revealed in 1999.
cases.d: The report of the inquiry into Madonna House, a Sisters of Charity residential centre for children, was completed and published by the Department of Health in 1996 with key sections removed. The withheld sections, revealed in May 1999, described beatings, humiliation and sexual assaults on children by a small number of staff, and management that failed to act on staff concerns and children's complaints.
cases.cite: Report on the Inquiry into the Operation of Madonna House (Department of Health, 1996); Irish Times, 13 May 1999

cases.n: Ireland — illegal birth registrations: St Patrick's Guild (126 cases) and the 2021 sampling review
cases.place: Dublin (St Patrick's Guild; Tusla; Adoption Authority of Ireland)
cases.victims_note: 126 illegal birth registrations confirmed at St Patrick's Guild (2018); the review estimated 5,540–19,980 adoption files may carry similar markers.
cases.who: St Patrick's Guild adoption society; Tusla and the Adoption Authority of Ireland (record holders); the Irish state
cases.d: In May 2018 the Irish government announced that 126 people placed through the St Patrick's Guild adoption society had been illegally registered as the birth children of their adoptive parents. An independent review then sampled 1,496 of about 150,000 adoption records; its report, published in March 2021, found about 265 files with suspicious markers and estimated 5,540 to 19,980 files might show similar signs. Tusla reported evidence of coerced consent, children placed abroad with little documentation and altered names and birth dates; the report did not recommend a full file review.
cases.cite: Independent review of incorrect birth registrations (Reynolds review), published March 2021; Irish Times Q&A, 10 March 2021

cases.n: Denmark — Appeals Board finds 'systematic illegal behaviour' in Korean adoptions 1970–1989
cases.victims_note: 7,220 children were adopted to Denmark from South Korea in 1970–1989; the report did not count affected cases.
cases.who: Danish adoption agencies DanAdopt and AC Børnehjælp (and Terre des Hommes); South Korean agencies
cases.cover: Two Danish agencies knew that children's information was being changed.
cases.d: A report released in January 2024 by Denmark's Appeals Board (Ankestyrelsen), which supervises intercountry adoption, examined adoptions from South Korea between 1970 and 1989, when 7,220 children were adopted to Denmark. It found 'systematic illegal behaviour' on the Korean side: weak regulation let organisations alter adoptees' identities and backgrounds in official documents, and large sums of money passed between organisations in the two countries. It found that DanAdopt and AC Børnehjælp knew about the changing of children's information. Adoptee groups said it did not examine the Danish state's role.
cases.cite: Ankestyrelsen report on adoptions from South Korea 1970–1989, January 2024; JURIST

cases.n: Denmark — state investigation of abuse in special-care institutions 1933–1980 (særforsorgen)
cases.place: Denmark (Ministry of Social Affairs; apology given at Horsens)
cases.victims_note: About 15,000 children and adults with disabilities were committed to the institutions; the sources do not give a count of children sexually abused.
cases.who: Danish state special-care institutions (særforsorgen) for children and adults with intellectual and physical disabilities
cases.d: An investigation ordered by the Danish government in 2020 and financed by the Ministry of Social and Senior Citizens, carried out with the University of Southern Denmark and published in 2022, found widespread abuse and neglect, including sexual assault, of children, young people and adults placed in state special-care institutions between 1933 and 1980. About 15,000 people with disabilities were committed. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen gave an official apology on 11 September 2023.
cases.cite: Historisk udredning vedrørende børn, unge og voksne anbragt i særforsorgens institutioner 1933–1980, 2022; The Local Denmark, 12 September 2023

cases.n: Iceland — Catholic Church investigative commission on Landakotsskóli (2012)
cases.victims_note: Of 30 former pupils and camp attendees questioned, 8 said they had been sexually abused and 27 described mental abuse.
cases.who: Catholic Church in Iceland; Landakotsskóli school and church summer camps
cases.cover: The commission reported that Bishop Joannes Gijsen destroyed a letter from a man who said the priest had abused him.
cases.d: An investigative commission of the Catholic Church in Iceland, chaired by Hjördís Hákonardóttir, reported in early November 2012. It confirmed that Rev. Ágúst Georg, principal of the church's Landakotsskóli school, and teacher Margrét Müller abused pupils. Of 30 former pupils and summer-camp children questioned, 8 said they had been sexually abused. It found that Bishop Joannes Gijsen destroyed a letter reporting abuse by the priest; Iceland later paid compensation for Landakotsskóli under a 2015 law.
cases.cite: Report of the investigative commission of the Catholic Church in Iceland, November 2012 (Iceland Review via BishopAccountability)

cases.n: Norway — NOU 2026:7 finds illegal and unethical intercountry adoptions
cases.victims_note: More than 20,000 children adopted to Norway since the 1950s; the committee examined the system and selected cases, not every adoption.
cases.who: Norwegian adoption organisations; Norwegian authorities; partner orphanages and bodies in 12 countries
cases.cover: Organisations did not always tell Norwegian authorities about payments or errors; authorities kept approving adoptions after learning of risks and illegalities.
cases.d: A government committee appointed on 20 June 2023 submitted NOU 2026:7 'Forsvarlighet, risiko og tillit' on 22 June 2026. Examining adoptions from 12 countries since the 1950s, it concluded there were illegal or unethical conditions and that Norwegian control was inadequate throughout. Individual findings included a kidnapped child adopted to Norway, a mother offered money to consent, and documents knowingly falsified; organisations made payments to orphanages that were sometimes linked to the number of children adopted.
cases.cite: NOU 2026:7 Forsvarlighet, risiko og tillit (Granskingsutvalget for utenlandsadopsjoner), 22 June 2026; summary for children published by the committee

cases.n: Finland — Conservative Laestadian movement (SRK) admits 70–100 child abuse cases mishandled
cases.victims_note: 70–100 cases of child sexual abuse within the movement since the 1980s, most within member families.
cases.who: Central Committee of Conservative Laestadian Congregations (SRK), Finland's largest revivalist movement within the Lutheran church
cases.cover: SRK admitted officials 'mishandled' cases, did not use expert help and did not communicate, which could look like downplaying or covering up.
cases.d: In April 2011 the SRK, which has about 35,000 members, announced that an internal report had found 70 to 100 cases of child sexual abuse within the movement since the 1980s. Most involved abuse within member families rather than by church officials, but the SRK admitted its officials had mishandled the cases and lacked the knowledge to respond. A study by Johanna Hurtig (University of Tampere) on abuse in the movement was published the same year.
cases.cite: SRK statement on internal report, April 2011 (AFP via TimesLive); Yle, 31 January 2022

notes:
Scope: UK (England, Wales, Scotland, NI, Jersey, Guernsey, Isle of Man), Ireland, Nordic countries incl. Greenland and Faroe.
Lists used: the IICSA list of 19 reports (gov.uk collection + IICSA site); the SCAI list of 16 findings volumes (SCAI news pages); NBSCCCI review tranches; the NOU and SOU lists. Bishop Accountability was used to find items, not cited.
Possible duplicates / updates for the merger:
- x-nor-nou-2026-7 updates nor-adoption-investigation (the existing record describes the 2023 launch; the committee reported NOU 2026:7 on 22 June 2026). Suggest merging, or keeping both with nor-adoption-investigation as the launch.
- gbr-scot-boarding-schools groups Fettes, Loretto, Gordonstoun, Merchiston and Edinburgh Academy. SCAI has published findings on Loretto (Apr 2023), Gordonstoun (Jun 2024), Merchiston (Jun 2025) and Fettes (Jan 2026), but NOT yet on Edinburgh Academy. The existing record's wording ("inquiry estimated about three quarters...") should be checked. Morrison's, Queen Victoria School and Keil are added as separate records.
- irl-raphoe-greene (convicted) is on the map; the NBSCCCI Raphoe review is in x-irl-nbsccci-diocesan-reviews.
- Islington: the existing record cites only the 2018 Morgan report; the 1995 White/Hart report was not opened.
- SCAI child migration: SCAI's site and STV both date Volume 1 to 21 March 2023 (not 2021).
Pending / no finding yet: SCAI foster care and boarding-out (hearings ended 1 Dec 2022; findings expected as the 17th volume); SCAI phase 8 (young offender institutions, secure care, List D schools); SCAI Edinburgh Academy; NI statutory public inquiry into mother and baby institutions; Ireland's Commission of Investigation into abuse in schools (after the 2024 Scoping Inquiry).
Gaps and items not confirmed:
- Guernsey and Faroe Islands: no official finding found.
- Iceland Vistheimilanefnd: in-scope finding not confirmed (see checklist). Breiðavík 2008 found violence and ill-treatment; compensation covered 1,190 applications.
- Norwegian municipal reviews after NOU 2004:23 (e.g. Bergen, Oslo, Trondheim): not researched; probably below the region reach rule.
- Denmark: Ankestyrelsen reports on other countries (e.g. Chile) and a 2025 statement on the Korean TRC were not opened. The Danish Catholic Church had police inquiries (2010) but no commissioned report was found.
- Sweden: no national church or sports-body finding found; Swedish Romani/Tornedalian commissions are out of scope (removal/assimilation).
- England: local CSE reviews below the reach rule were not listed (e.g. Derby SCR 2010, Bristol SCR 2016, Kirklees/Huddersfield). Bristol is covered in the IICSA networks report. The Charity Commission's Watch Tower Britain inquiry was not checked.
- Shaw report: publication month (November 2007) is inferred from a Times article archived under 23 Nov 2007; the Scotsman piece is undated.
- CEOP 2011: the Yorkshire Post gives 2,379 as offenders; other summaries give it as potential victims. The record states the number as 'cases' to avoid the conflict.
- Finland SRK 2011 was an internal report, not an independent commission. Kept as a borderline item because it is a national religious movement admitting institutional mishandling.
- McLellan Commission (Scotland) was kept and the Nolan/Cumberlege/Elliott reviews (England and Wales) were excluded. Both are safeguarding-structure reviews, but McLellan states that serious abuse occurred and describes a culture of denial. Borderline call.
